It can't be a place where older kids quietly dominate younger kids, or where secrecy is treated as a sign of independence.

community-s8g1/u2.input:
Give children real agency. Their "no" matters, and no grownup has a right to a kid's affection, physical contact, obedience beyond legitimate safety needs, or private access to them.

Create a no-secrets rule. No grownup has the right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or another adult they trust. This applies to gifts, games, touch, conversations and relationships. A surprise is different because at the end of a certain date, the surprise has to be told. Secrets meant to isolate the kid are forbidden.
community-s8g1/u2.A:
Allow kids to say no. No grownup has a right to a kid’s affection, body, obedience (outside of legitimate needs of the adult to keep the kid safe, as the adult is legally bound to do) or privacy.

Adopt a rule of no secrets. No grownup has a right to ask a kid to keep a secret from his mom or other trusted adults. This includes things like gifts, playing games with the kid, touching the kid, or having certain kinds of conversations and relationships with the kid. A surprise can be okay, because at the end of a certain date, the surprise has to be told. But isolating a kid with secrets is not okay.
community-s8g1/u2.B:
Let kids say “No”. Nobody has the right of taking a kid’s affection, of touching them, of ordering them (outside of legitimate needs of the kid) or of being alone with them.

Create the “No secret rule”: nobody has the right to order kids to keep secrets from their mom or any other trusted adult for them. This is valid for gifts, games, touch, talks or relations with that person. A surprise isn’t a secret, because at the end of a certain date, it has to be told. It’s not allowed to isolate kids with secrets.

community-s8g1/u3.input: Teach truthfulness before there's a crisis. The kids should know that telling the truth is important, that their words have power, and that adults will take what they say seriously. Don't interrogate them, punish them for not being sure, or dismiss what they report. A scared or confused kid may tell the story "wrong" and still need protecting.
community-s8g1/u3.A: Have previous conversations with them about the importance of telling the truth, the power of their words, and how even if they say something and it seems untrue, that it will be taken seriously. Do not interrogate them, do not make them feel bad if they’re not sure, and don’t brush it off if they are telling it wrong – they may still need protection.
community-s8g1/u3.B: The best thing to do is to teach kids from the beginning that telling the truth is incredibly important, to take in their words seriously, but not to interrogate them or to punish them if it turns out that they didn’t tell the truth. The kid might have told the truth in his own mind, but if he doesn’t know how to tell the story “right”, he still needs to be protected.

community-s8g1/u4.input: Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. Make sure there's at least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route they can reach without going through the community's leadership. As the 1984 Island Pond raid showed, state intervention can fail spectacularly. Vermont authorities seized 112 children, only to have a court reject the state's blanket request and order their return. Enclosing them completely within the community can fail too. Kids need more than one world.
community-s8g1/u4.A: Make sure the kids have relationships with people outside the community and a way to report bad things to people outside the community. Let them have relationships with grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers, etc. who can give them a sense of how their life is going compared to others their age. Make sure there's at least one person that they trust who will advocate for them if things go bad or a way for them to report bad things going on in the community to the outside world. The lesson of the 1984 Island Pond raid is that counting on the state to fix things doesn't work; in that case the state swooped in and seized 112 children, and when the state's blanket request to take the kids was rejected by a court, put them all right back in. Just enclosing them in the community doesn't work, they need to have more than one world.
community-s8g1/u4.B: Make sure they have some relationships outside the community, even if it's just with grandparents, cousins, local friends or teachers. That will help them get some perspective on their lives. Make sure there is at least one adult they can trust, or some other way for them to advocate for themselves or report abuse, that doesn't involve the community's leadership. Learning from history is always a good idea. In 1984 the state raided Island Pond, removing 112 kids, but the state's blanket request was rejected by a court and the kids were returned. Trying to enclose them, too, didn't work. Make sure they have more than one world.

community-s8g1/u6.input:
The Amish let their young people decide on their own whether to join the church once they're adults, and roughly 85 percent or more eventually do. Popular culture tends to blow Rumspringa out of proportion, as if every teenager went wild, but adult baptism still matters, because it makes belonging a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.

If the children never leave, the community can't know whether they'd come back freely. So let them study, travel, make friends, see other ways of life, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors.
community-s8g1/u6.A:
The Amish actually allow their youth to leave, and take up to about 85%+ back in when they are older and have made up their own minds to join the church. Rumspringa is largely exaggerated by popular culture, but the fact that they are not baptized until adulthood is very important.

If the kids never leave, there's no way of knowing if they'd ever come back, so why not let them leave. Let them learn, explore, meet friends, and say that the founder was wrong about something.
community-s8g1/u6.B:
The Amish allow their children to leave - however a fairly large percent (85% or more) decide to join the church when they are of age. The Rumspringa aspect seems to be exaggerated by pop culture, but the fact that they are still being baptised as an adult is key.

If the kids never leave, how can they come back ? If the kids want to study and see the world, why not let them ? If they want to befriend other people, why not ? If they want to disagree with the founding fathers of their religion, why should they be considered as traitors ?

community-s8g1/u7.input: The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's just not making it artificially impossible for people to leave. And if kids grow up without ever using money, they especially need an education about how the money world works, and what to do when they have to deal with it. Part of that is knowing about jobs, rent, contracts, banking, scams, ID and getting around, and how to ask for help when they need it. They also need transferable skills and education, relationships outside the community, access to their records and documents, and at least one plausible next step, like school, an apprenticeship, work, family or another community. If the community has the resources to help out with temporary housing, travel, tools or a small reserve for the transition, great. But even if it doesn't, it can at least avoid punishing people for leaving, or withholding the knowledge and records a young adult needs to function somewhere else. No upbringing can be completely free, and there will always be some path dependence, but belonging doesn't have to be turned into a trap.
community-s8g1/u7.A: Well, if all the standard for realistic is that it doesn't actively make it impossible for people to leave, then yeah that's doable. It would be a good idea to prepare kids who've grown up without ever using money for the possibility that they might have to deal with the money world outside, by teaching them about it. Things like what kind of jobs exist, how to get a place to live, what contracts/banking/scams/ID/travel are, and how to ask for help if they need it. Making sure they have easily transferable skills and education, relationships outside the community, access to their records and important documents, and some ideas of what they might want to do next (school, apprenticeship, job, family, other community, whatever). If the community has the resources it could also provide some assistance for temporary housing/travel/tools/etc. If not, it can at least not make things harder for someone who wants to leave. No one can have a totally free upbringing and be completely free from path dependence, but it's possible to not trap people.
community-s8g1/u7.B: The bar isn’t "unlimited freedom", the bar is “not actively making it impossible for people to leave” . And for kids who have never seen the money world, yeah, it would make sense for them to get a decent education and know-how of how the money world operates, what to do if they need to deal with the money world. How to deal with jobs, rent, contracts, banks, scams, ID, transport, how to access help, etc. Have some transferable skills, education. Have some relations outside of the community. Access to all of their records, documents, etc. Have some idea of what to do next: school, apprenticeship, job, family, other community, etc. If the community has the financial ability to give them a helping hand (temporary housing, transport, tools, or whatever), that would be nice, but if they don’t, just not actively making it harder for people to leave is enough. Obviously they can’t have completely free upbringing, there will always be some path dependency.

It's quite possible some of them will leave for good, or start their own communities with different values instead of waiting decades to inherit the original one. Parents may feel that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.

Couples sharing a home, a culture and a bed still split over different ideas about screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. Multiply that by twenty adults with twenty different experiences of how they were brought up.

Goodwill doesn't answer those questions once kids are living in the middle of the disagreement. There need to be enough shared principles about kids to give the community coherence, and enough space for parents to be parents.
community-s8g1/u8.A:

Couples living together, sharing the same culture and the same bed, often split apart over disagreements about how to raise children. How, then, can a community containing 20 adults with 20 different backgrounds of being raised themselves, deal with the issues of screen time, vaccinations, schooling, religious upbringing, diet, child discipline, and medical care, to name a few?

This can't be done on goodwill alone. There must be sufficient agreement on principles regarding children for the community to be coherent, and enough freedom for parents to parent.
community-s8g1/u8.B:
It's possible that some of them will split off, either permanently, or into their own communities with different values, rather than wait until they inherit the community. And some of their parents may experience that as loss.

Marriages of people who live in the same house, in the same culture and even sleep in the same bed, split apart over disagreements on television, vaccination, schooling, religion, food, discipline, medical care, etc. Now, imagine twenty adults with twenty different experiences of what a good upbringing looks like.

Good will only takes a community so far when kids are involved. There needs to be some balance between common principles around kids, and allowing parents to be parents.
